written_by: SENTINEL editors, revised from the earlier dashboard account; facts checked and extended to October 2026 by web search on 16 October 2026
lede: Washington's role in the region's civil–military relations no longer runs through aid tables alone. Grants, officer training, basing, detention, coalition-building and, since 2025, direct military action form one continuum of leverage, and this page reads them together.

caribbean.title: From the Caribbean campaign to the Shield of the Americas
intro: Since January 2025 the United States has moved from aid conditionality and multilateral frameworks to direct coercion in the hemisphere: a terrorist frame for criminal groups, lethal strikes at sea, a forward military build-up, and in January 2026 the capture of Venezuela's president in Caracas.

In 2026 the campaign was given a standing form. Washington recognized the interim government in Caracas, launched a counter-cartel coalition with 18 regional partners, and in August replaced the ad hoc Operation Southern Spear with a permanent Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere.

timeline.title: Guantánamo opened to migrants
timeline.text: A presidential memorandum ordered the naval base's migrant operations center expanded to hold up to 30,000 people. In practice it held far fewer: about 500 had passed through by June 2025, usually a few dozen at a time.

timeline.title: Cartels designated as terrorists
timeline.text: Eight Latin American groups were designated foreign terrorist organizations on 20 February; the list reached 21 by September 2026.

timeline.title: Deportees sent to El Salvador's CECOT
timeline.text: More than 200 Venezuelans accused of belonging to Tren de Aragua were flown to the CECOT mega-prison under the Alien Enemies Act. In July 2025 they were returned to Venezuela in an exchange for ten detained Americans; Caracas put the number at 252.

timeline.title: Strikes at sea begin
timeline.text: The US military began striking boats it said were carrying drugs, first in the Caribbean and later, mostly, in the eastern Pacific. The campaign was named Operation Southern Spear in November 2025. By 4 October 2026 at least 238 people had been killed in at least 79 strikes. The Pentagon has not shown that those on board were trafficking drugs.

timeline.title: Roosevelt Roads reopened
timeline.text: The former naval station in Puerto Rico, closed since 2004, was reactivated for F-35B fighters, drones and maritime patrol aircraft. More than 10,000 US personnel were in the Southern Command area by November, with the carrier USS Gerald R. Ford on its way.

timeline.title: A new force for Haiti
timeline.text: The UN Security Council authorized a 5,500-strong Gang Suppression Force with powers of arrest to replace the Kenyan-led mission. By July 2026 only about 1,100 troops had arrived.

match.terms: Gang Suppression|GSF|Force de r[ée]pression|Fuerza de Supresi

timeline.title: Ecuador rejects foreign bases
timeline.text: Voters turned down President Noboa's proposal to allow foreign military bases, 60.6% to 39.4%, a setback for plans to bring US forces back to Manta.

timeline.title: Cartel de los Soles designated
timeline.text: The State Department designated the network it says is headed by Nicolás Maduro a foreign terrorist organization, effective 24 November.

match.terms: Cartel de los Soles|Cártel de los Soles

timeline.title: Operation Absolute Resolve
timeline.text: US forces captured Nicolás Maduro and Cilia Flores in Caracas on 3 January. Both pleaded not guilty in New York to narco-terrorism and cocaine charges; trial is set for June 2027. Delcy Rodríguez was sworn in as acting president on 5 January.

timeline.title: An oil squeeze on Cuba
timeline.text: Executive Order 14380 (29 January) declared a national emergency over Cuba and authorized tariffs on any country that supplies it with oil. By October US agencies were intercepting fuel cargoes bound for the island.

timeline.title: El Mencho killed in Jalisco
timeline.text: Mexican forces killed the Jalisco cartel's leader, Nemesio Oseguera, on 22 February in an operation supported by a US military-led intelligence task force. Cartel road blockades followed across several states.

timeline.title: Joint strikes in Ecuador
timeline.text: US and Ecuadorian forces bombed a camp of the Comandos de la Frontera near the Colombian border in early March, the first acknowledged US combat action in South America since Caracas.

timeline.title: Shield of the Americas
timeline.text: Twelve regional leaders met President Trump at Doral on 7 March to launch an anti-cartel coalition, the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition. The same day Washington recognized Delcy Rodríguez's government; the US embassy in Caracas reopened on 14 March and she replaced the defence minister, Vladimir Padrino López, on 18 March.

match.terms: Shield of the Americas|Escudo de las Am[eé]ricas|Counter.?Cartel|Anticártel|A3C|Padrino|embajada de (EE|Estados)

timeline.title: Tren de Aragua leader killed
timeline.text: President Trump said a US strike on a compound in Venezuela had killed Tren de Aragua's leader, Héctor "Niño" Guerrero. Caracas described a joint operation.

timeline.title: A permanent task force
timeline.text: Southern Command activated Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere on 4 August to run operations with the coalition's 18 partners. It succeeded Operation Southern Spear and is designed as a standing headquarters.

match.terms: Joint Task Force|Fuerza de Tarea Conjunta|Southern Spear|Lanza del Sur

timeline.title: Colombia changes course
timeline.text: Abelardo de la Espriella took office on 7 August promising a crackdown on armed groups. Washington announced its intention to provide $1 billion in security assistance, pending Congress, and Colombia joined the coalition days later.

timeline.title: Lasers on the border
timeline.text: The US military used a high-energy laser to bring down three cartel drones in the Rio Grande Valley. By early September it said it had downed more than 300 cartel drones along the border in 2026.

timeline.title: The coalition in New York
timeline.text: Fifteen governments met on 22 September during the UN General Assembly and adopted a joint communiqué widening the Shield's agenda to economic security and multilateral coordination.

match.terms: Shield of the Americas|Escudo de las Am[eé]ricas|aliados en Latinoam|Counter.?Cartel

timeline.title: Haiti force launched
timeline.text: With its mandate extended to March 2027, the Gang Suppression Force was formally launched on 8 October at about 1,500 personnel, under a third of its authorized strength.

match.terms: Gang Suppression|GSF|Force de r[ée]pression|Fuerza de Supresi

timeline.title: Sanctions eased on Caracas
timeline.text: The Treasury removed National Assembly president Jorge Rodríguez from its sanctions list on 14 October, six months after his sister was delisted and weeks after President Trump announced a deal giving the United States control of 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan oil reserves.

assessment: The 2025–26 operations mark a structural shift in US posture in the hemisphere, from institution-building and aid conditionality towards direct coercion, transactional bilateral deals and a coalition built around the cartel threat. The capture of a sitting head of state in his own capital has no post-1989 precedent, and the speed with which Washington then recognized, delisted and traded oil access with his successors shows that regime change was not the aim; leverage was.

For civil–military relations the lessons are uneven. Armed forces loyal to a sanctioned leader learned that loyalty does not buy sovereignty. Governments that joined the coalition gained intelligence, equipment and political cover for militarized policing, while the new permanent task force makes US operational involvement a standing feature rather than a crisis response. SENTINEL's assessment is that the net effect on regional civil–military norms is destabilizing: it may shorten some authoritarian tenures while normalizing extralegal executive force and weakening legislative oversight of security policy on both sides.

access.title: The access network
access.note: Not only bases: a regional network that links detention, surveillance flights, logistics, counternarcotics patrols and crisis response across the Caribbean basin and northern South America.

channels_note: Military and counternarcotics money reaches the region through distinct funding accounts, each with its own legal authority and oversight. International Narcotics Control and Law Enforcement (INCLE) and Foreign Military Financing (FMF) are the largest. International Military Education and Training (IMET) is small but reaches almost every country, and is the channel most studied for its effect on officers' attitudes to civilian control. Defense Department accounts, among them the Section 333 train-and-equip authority, let the Pentagon fund partner forces directly, without a State Department lead, and are reported with a longer lag. For fiscal 2027 the administration asked Congress to cut State Department funding by about a quarter while steering almost half of worldwide narcotics-control money, $535 million, to Latin America and the Caribbean; the House bill passed in July funds that account well above the request.
